full_title: JUDGE JAIME B. SANTIAGO, COMPLAINANT, VS. ROMELITO G. FERNANDO, UTILITY WORKER I, BRANCH 18, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, [RTC], TAGAYTAY CITY, CAVITE, RESPONDENT.
docket: A.M. No. P-22-053 (Formerly OCA IPI No. 15-4466-P)
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)
topics: Revised Rule 140 applies to all pending cases regardless of when the infraction was committed
Jurisdiction not lost by separation from service (AWOL, dropping from the rolls) during pendency
Gross insubordination: defying the presiding judge, and failing to comment despite OCA directives
Court employee receiving money from a litigant is grave (gross) misconduct
Separate penalties for multiple offenses; penalties in lieu of dismissal (Revised Rule 140, Secs. 18 and 21)

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 2. Discipline

doctrine:
**Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, effective April 4, 2022) governs all pending and future administrative cases against Judiciary personnel, regardless of when the infractions were committed** (Section 24). It is a disciplinary framework wholly independent of the Civil Service rules.

**Once the Court acquires jurisdiction over an administrative case, it is not lost because the respondent leaves the service while the case is pending** (here, by going on AWOL and being dropped from the rolls). What matters is that the case was instituted while the respondent was still in the service. A respondent's failure to comment does not prevent the Court from imposing sanctions; under Section 3(3) it is a waiver of participation, and the case proceeds on the available evidence. Silence in the face of serious accusations may be taken as an implied admission (*qui tacet consentire videtur*).

**Gross insubordination**, the "inexplicable and unjustified refusal to obey some order that a superior is entitled to give and have obeyed," covers (a) a court employee's repeated disregard of the presiding judge's directives to transmit pleadings and case records promptly, and (b) willful failure to file a comment despite the OCA's directives, which is defiance of the Court itself. **A court employee's receipt of money from a litigant, whatever the reason and even if the litigant approached him, is grave misconduct**, now termed gross misconduct constituting a violation of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel (Canon I, Sec. 2). Both are serious charges under Section 14(a) and (n). Under **Section 21, a separate penalty is imposed for each offense** arising from separate acts in one proceeding. Where dismissal can no longer be imposed because of a supervening separation, **Section 18** allows forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits) and disqualification **"and/or"** a fine, so either or both may be imposed.
facts:
Romelito G. Fernando was a Utility Worker I at RTC Branch 18, Tagaytay City. In December 2014 the Acting Presiding Judge, Jaime B. Santiago, appointed him Clerk III in charge of civil cases. In an August 11, 2015 complaint, Judge Santiago charged him with insubordination, irregularity in the performance of duty, and gross neglect of duty. Despite repeated admonitions and written warnings, Fernando had failed to refer to the judge the formal offers of evidence in two land registration cases (filed October 10, 2014 and February 17, 2015), giving them to him only on August 11, 2015. In his comment, Fernando blamed his workload and his co-employees.

In an October 5, 2015 supplemental complaint, Judge Santiago charged him with continued irregularities, gross incompetence, and gross misconduct. On September 18, 2015, Mrs. Lolita Borja came to court looking for Fernando. She said he had asked for PHP 40,000.00 to facilitate the bail of her son, detained for violation of Section 11 of RA 9165, but her son remained in jail. A handwritten note signed "Rommel Fernando" acknowledged receipt of PHP 35,000.00 "for safekeeping" on May 12, 2015, plus PHP 5,000.00 on May 22, 2015. During a January 2014 inventory, 51 criminal case folders and one Juvenile and Domestic Relations Court case folder were found in his work area. Three more criminal case folders were later found in his custody, and the missing records of two land registration cases turned up in his steel drawer.

The OCA directed Fernando to comment on the supplemental complaint. He asked for and was granted an extension until March 29, 2016, citing health reasons, but he never filed a comment, even after a January 16, 2017 tracer with a final warning. He last logged in on January 22, 2016 and went on AWOL. On November 29, 2017, his name was dropped from the rolls. The OCA recommended that he be found guilty of gross insubordination and grave misconduct and, since dismissal could no longer be imposed, that he suffer forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits) and perpetual disqualification from re-employment in government.
issues: Whether Revised Rule 140 governs the case, and whether respondent may still be held liable despite being dropped from the rolls and despite his failure to file a comment.
Whether respondent is guilty of gross insubordination and grave (gross) misconduct.
ruling:
**1. Yes, Revised Rule 140 applies, and the Court retains jurisdiction.** Revised Rule 140, effective April 4, 2022, was meant to be a disciplinary framework for the entire Judiciary, independent of the Civil Service rules and applicable to all pending and future cases regardless of when the infractions were committed (Section 24). **Respondent's absence without leave during the pendency of the case does not prevent the Court from determining his liability:** jurisdiction, once attached, is not lost because the employee is no longer in office, and what is essential is that the case was instituted while he was still in the service. His failure to comment does not prevent sanctions either (Section 3(3): waiver of participation, with the investigation proceeding on the evidence).

**2. Yes, two counts of gross insubordination and one count of gross misconduct.** *First count:* judges must supervise their personnel and stamp out irregularities. Judge Santiago acted within his authority in requiring prompt transmittal of pleadings and records. Even without proof of corruption, respondent's repeated disobedience delayed the disposition of cases ("justice delayed is justice denied"). *Second count:* respondents in administrative cases must comment on the accusations, as part of their duty to preserve the integrity of the Judiciary. Respondent ignored the OCA's 1st Indorsement even after asking for and getting an extension, then went on AWOL. This was willful disrespect for the OCA, through which the Court supervised lower court personnel, and so **defiance of the lawful orders of the Court itself.** Given the gravity of the accusations, his silence was contrary to human experience. Citing Yoshimura v. Panagsagan, the Court deduced "his implicit admission of the charges," so the withholding of records and the receipt of money stood undisputed.

*Gross misconduct:* grave misconduct is a serious transgression of an established rule that threatens the administration of justice, and it may manifest as corruption. Canon I, Section 2 of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel bars court employees from soliciting or accepting any gift, favor, or benefit on the understanding that it will influence their official actions. Respondent had no authority to collect PHP 40,000.00 from Mrs. Borja. His liability did not rest on silence alone: the signed handwritten receipt stood uncontroverted, and the spouses Borja's statements in the judge's investigation detailed how he promised, for PHP 40,000.00, to take care of their son's bail. **That the Borjas approached him first is no excuse; "the sole act of receiving money from litigants, whatever the reason may be, is antithesis to being a court employee."** Grave misconduct is the same as gross misconduct, which is a serious charge under Section 14(a).

**3. Separate penalties for each offense.** All three offenses are serious charges, punishable under Section 17(1) by dismissal, suspension of more than six months up to one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000.00 up to PHP 200,000.00. Under Section 21, separate penalties are imposed for separate offenses. Because respondent had been dropped from the rolls, dismissal could no longer be imposed, so Section 18 applied. **Its "and/or" authorizes either or both of its penalties.** The Court modified the OCA's recommendation as follows: the first count of gross insubordination was penalized under Section 18(a) (forfeiture and disqualification), and the second count of gross insubordination and the gross misconduct were each penalized with a PHP 150,000.00 fine. Under Section 22, the fine is payable within three months. If unpaid, it may be deducted from his salaries and benefits, including accrued leave credits.
disposition: Respondent Romelito G. Fernando was found GUILTY of two counts of GROSS INSUBORDINATION and one count of GROSS MISCONDUCT constituting a violation of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel. Under Section 18(a) of Revised Rule 140, he was meted forfeiture of all benefits, except accrued leave credits, and disqualification from reinstatement or appointment to any public office, including GOCCs. He was ordered to pay an aggregate FINE of PHP 300,000.00 within three months from promulgation; if unpaid, it is to be deducted from his salaries and benefits, including accrued leave credits. He was also ordered to RETURN PHP 40,000.00 to Mrs. Lolita Borja, with 6% interest per annum from finality of the Resolution until full payment.

bar_questions.q: Lito, a court stenographer, received PHP 30,000.00 from Mrs. Dela Cruz, whose son was detained for a drug offense, after promising to "fix" the son's bail papers. The son was never released. Charged administratively, Lito admitted signing a receipt for the money. He argued that (1) Mrs. Dela Cruz approached him first and begged for help, and (2) he only held the money "for safekeeping" and never promised to influence any judge. Is Lito administratively liable?

alac.answer: Yes. Lito is liable for grave misconduct, now designated gross misconduct constituting a violation of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel.
alac.legal_basis: Grave misconduct is a serious transgression of an established rule of action that tends to threaten the administration of justice, and it may manifest as corruption. Canon I, Section 2 of the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel prohibits court employees from soliciting or accepting any gift, favor, or benefit on the understanding that it will influence their official actions. A court employee's act of soliciting or receiving money from litigants is grave misconduct. "[T]he sole act of receiving money from litigants, whatever the reason may be, is antithesis to being a court employee," and it is no defense that the litigant approached the employee first. Gross misconduct is a serious charge under Section 14(a) of Revised Rule 140. (Judge Santiago v. Fernando, A.M. No. P-22-053, January 17, 2023)
alac.application: Lito, a court employee, admittedly received PHP 30,000.00 from the mother of a detained accused after promising to facilitate bail. He had no authority or legal basis to collect that money. Calling it "safekeeping" changes nothing, since the mere receipt of money from a litigant is the offense. That Mrs. Dela Cruz sought him out does not exculpate him either.
alac.conclusion: Lito is guilty of gross misconduct and may be dismissed from the service.

bar_questions.q: Rosa, a clerk at an RTC branch, was administratively charged in 2024 with withholding case records. Before filing her comment, she stopped reporting for work, and the Court dropped her from the rolls for being absent without official leave. She never filed a comment. (a) Has the Court lost jurisdiction to decide the administrative case? (b) If Rosa is found guilty of serious offenses warranting dismissal, may the Court impose both forfeiture of benefits with disqualification and a fine?

alac.answer: (a) No. The Court retains jurisdiction. (b) Yes. In lieu of dismissal, the Court may impose either or both of the alternative penalties.
alac.legal_basis: Jurisdiction over an administrative case, once acquired, is not lost because the respondent is no longer in office while the case is pending; what is essential is that the case was instituted while the respondent was still in the service. Failure to file a comment results in waiver of participation, and the case proceeds on the available evidence (Revised Rule 140, Sec. 3(3)). Under Section 18 of Revised Rule 140, if dismissal can no longer be imposed because of a supervening separation (except death), the respondent may be meted (a) forfeiture of all or part of the benefits (never accrued leave credits) and disqualification from reinstatement or appointment to any public office, "and/or" (b) a fine. The "and/or" authorizes either or both. (Judge Santiago v. Fernando, A.M. No. P-22-053, January 17, 2023)
alac.application: The complaint was filed in 2024 while Rosa was still a court employee, so the Court's jurisdiction had attached. Her later AWOL and dropping from the rolls do not divest it, and her failure to comment simply waives her participation. Because dismissal can no longer be carried out, Section 18 applies. As in Santiago, where the Court imposed forfeiture and disqualification for one count and fines for two other counts, the Court may combine both penalties. Under Section 21, it imposes a separate penalty for each offense.
alac.conclusion: The Court may still decide the case and may impose forfeiture, disqualification, and a fine against Rosa.

bar_questions.q: The OCA directed Ben, a court process server, to comment on a complaint accusing him of extorting money from litigants. Ben asked for a 15-day extension, which was granted, but he never filed a comment, even after a tracer with a final warning. (a) Is Ben's failure to comment an administrative offense separate from the charge of extortion? (b) What is the effect of his silence on the extortion charge, and how will the penalties be imposed if he is found liable on both?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. His willful failure to comment despite the OCA's directives is a separate offense of gross insubordination. (b) His silence may be taken as an implied admission of the extortion charge, and the Court will impose a separate penalty for each offense.
alac.legal_basis: Gross insubordination is the "inexplicable and unjustified refusal to obey some order that a superior is entitled to give and have obeyed." A respondent's willful refusal to comply with the OCA's directive to comment is disrespect of the OCA, through which the Court supervises lower court personnel, and so defiance of the Court's own lawful orders. When a respondent stays silent despite serious accusations, the Court may deduce an implied admission (qui tacet consentire videtur). Under Section 21 of Revised Rule 140, when a respondent is liable for more than one offense arising from separate acts in a single proceeding, a separate penalty is imposed for each. (Judge Santiago v. Fernando, A.M. No. P-22-053, January 17, 2023, citing Yoshimura v. Panagsagan)
alac.application: Ben acknowledged the OCA's directive by asking for, and getting, an extension. He then ignored both the directive and the final warning. That is willful defiance, a separate act from the alleged extortion, and so a separate count of gross insubordination. Faced with an accusation as serious as extortion, an innocent employee would naturally deny it. His silence lets the Court treat the charge as admitted, especially if other evidence such as receipts or witness statements supports it. If found liable for both, he receives one penalty for the insubordination and another for the misconduct.
alac.conclusion: Ben's failure to comment is a separate offense of gross insubordination, his silence may be taken as an admission, and separate penalties will be imposed for each offense.

notes: The caption describes respondent as Utility Worker I, but the Resolution says Judge Santiago appointed him Clerk III in December 2014, and the dropping-from-the-rolls matter (A.M. No. 17-10-252-RTC) refers to him as Clerk III. Marquez, J., took no part because of prior action as Court Administrator. This Resolution applied Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC), and the peso ranges quoted are those of Revised Rule 140. The later 2026 decisions in this topic say that the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability superseded Rule 140 as to judges. The 2027 syllabus also lists a 2025 Code of Conduct and Accountability for Court Officials and Personnel (A.M. No. 25-06-11-SC). Check that code's current penalty provisions before relying on these amounts for court personnel.
